common_name: Apple Blossom Caladium (Pale Pink-and-White Speckled Fancy Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Apple Blossom bears pale pink-and-white leaves finely speckled with darker pink.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Apple Blossom bears large, heart-shaped leaves in a delicate pale pink-and-white blend finely speckled with deeper pink, edged in green, a softer, more pastel-toned fancy-leaf caladium than the bold reds many gardeners associate with the genus. It provides months of reliable, low-maintenance color in shaded beds, borders, and containers without needing flowers, pairing especially well with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Party Punch Caladium (Dwarf Hot Pink Sun-Tolerant Strap-Leaf Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Party Punch is a dwarf strap-leaf caladium bred for sun tolerance in containers, with hot pink centers and red veining.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to nearly full sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. Party Punch bears vivid hot pink centers with contrasting red veining on narrow strap-shaped leaves, on a dwarf, compact plant bred specifically for reliable sun performance in containers and mixed plantings. Its small stature and bright, saturated color make it a strong choice for pots, window boxes, and the front of a shaded or partly sunny border. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: White Pearl Caladium (Compact Creamy-White Green-Veined Strap-Leaf Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; White Pearl is a compact strap-leaf caladium with creamy white leaves and contrasting green veins, tolerating part sun.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. White Pearl bears creamy white, narrow strap-shaped leaves with contrasting green veins, glowing brightly in a shaded bed and providing a cool, luminous contrast to darker-leaved companions. Its compact size fits containers, edging, and small-scale plantings. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: White Majesty Caladium (Large White Strap-Leaf Caladium with Bold Veins)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; White Majesty bears large white strap-type leaves with prominent green veins, more sun-tolerant than fancy white caladium types.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to filtered sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. White Majesty bears large white leaves marked with prominent, bold green veining, a brighter, more sun-tolerant option than the classic fancy-leaf white caladiums that require deeper shade to avoid scorch. Its bold, luminous foliage lights up a shaded or lightly filtered-sun bed through the growing season. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Tiki Torch Caladium (Flame-Patterned Red-Orange Sun-Tolerant Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Tiki Torch is a sun-tolerant strap-leaf caladium with flame-like red-orange coloring radiating up the leaf.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to nearly full sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. Tiki Torch bears vivid red-orange coloring that radiates up each narrow, strap-shaped leaf in a flame-like pattern, a fiery, warm-toned caladium well suited to sunnier spots than most fancy-leaf selections tolerate. Its bold color and sun tolerance make it a strong choice for containers and mixed beds that get more than dappled light. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Starburst Caladium (White Strap-Leaf with Radiating Red Speckles)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Starburst is a sun-tolerant white strap-leaf caladium with red speckles radiating outward from the leaf center.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to nearly full sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. Starburst bears a white leaf background flecked with red speckles that radiate outward from the center like a burst of sparks, a lively speckled pattern distinct from the more solid-colored strap-leaf cultivars. Its bright, patterned foliage and sun tolerance make it a strong choice for containers and mixed beds. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Sangria Caladium (Compact Wine-Red Sun-Tolerant Strap-Leaf Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Sangria is a compact, sun-tolerant strap-leaf caladium with wine-red leaves and darker veining.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to nearly full sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. Sangria bears deep wine-red leaves with darker veining on a compact, sun-tolerant plant, providing rich, saturated color in containers and mixed beds that get more light than fancy-leaf caladiums can handle. Its small stature suits pots, window boxes, and the front of a border. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Fallen City Caladium (Dark Green Fancy-Leaf with Deep Red Speckling)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Fallen City bears dark green fancy-leaf foliage heavily speckled with deep red splotches, best in partial shade.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Fallen City bears dark green fancy-leaf foliage heavily speckled and splotched with deep red across the leaf surface, a bold, richly patterned combination that stands apart from the more uniform coloring of many fancy-leaf caladium cultivars. It provides months of reliable, low-maintenance color in shaded beds, borders, and containers without needing flowers, pairing especially well with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Rudicundum Caladium (Heirloom Dark Green with Purple Veins and Pink Spots)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Rudicundum is an heirloom fancy-leaf caladium with dark green leaves, purple veins, and pink spotting, a shade lover.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Rudicundum, a long-cultivated heirloom fancy-leaf cultivar, bears dark green leaves marked with distinctive purple veining and scattered pink spotting, a subtler, more muted color combination than the boldly contrasting reds and whites of many modern caladiums. Its old-fashioned coloring and long cultivation history make it a favorite among collectors seeking heirloom caladium varieties. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Tea Cup Elephant Ear (Compact Cupped-Leaf Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Tea Cup is a smaller-statured sport of Coffee Cups with shiny green cupped leaves forming a distinct bowl shape, well suited to containers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9. Tea Cup, a smaller-statured sport of the popular Coffee Cups elephant ear, bears glossy green leaves with strongly upturned margins forming a pronounced cup shape that collects rainwater, on a plant scaled down enough to suit large containers where full-sized Coffee Cups would be too big. The cupped leaves shimmer and hold water in dappled light, creating a living water feature and wildlife attraction on a more manageable scale. The plant spreads readily by stolons; divide every two to three years to control spread, and provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Colocasia Cultivars for Florida
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Elephant Ear Varieties for Louisiana
North Carolina State Extension — Colocasia in Southern Gardens

common_name: Pharaoh's Mask Elephant Ear (Green Leaf with Bold Black Hand-Painted Veins)

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Pharaoh's Mask bears green leaves with bold, raised black midribs and veins that look hand-painted, a striking pattern among elephant ear cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9. Pharaoh's Mask bears large green leaves crossed with bold, raised, near-black midribs and veins that stand out sharply against the lighter leaf surface, giving the foliage a dramatic, almost hand-painted appearance unlike the more uniformly colored leaves of most colocasia cultivars. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every two to three years to control spread. Provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions, as elephant ear grows naturally along streamsides and in boggy areas.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Colocasia Cultivars for Florida

common_name: Waikiki Elephant Ear (Green Leaf with Dark Maroon Center Blotch)

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Waikiki, part of the Royal Hawaiian series, bears green leaves with a dramatic dark maroon-burgundy center blotch, tolerating partial shade to shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9. Waikiki, part of the Royal Hawaiian elephant ear series, bears bright green leaves marked with a dramatic dark maroon-burgundy blotch radiating from the center, a bold two-tone pattern that makes a strong focal point in a shaded bog garden or large container. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every two to three years to control spread. Provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions, as elephant ear grows naturally along streamsides and in boggy areas.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Colocasia Cultivars for Florida

common_name: Black Ruffles Elephant Ear (Dark Purple-Black Wavy-Margined Colocasia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Black Ruffles bears dark purple-black leaves with pronounced wavy, ruffled margins, a textured take on the popular dark-leaved colocasia group.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9. Black Ruffles bears deep purple-black leaves with pronounced wavy, ruffled margins, giving the dramatic dark foliage a textured, crinkled edge unlike the smoother leaves of most other black-leaved colocasia cultivars. Its dark, ruffled leaves make a striking contrast against lighter-colored companion plants in a shaded bog garden or large container. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every two to three years to control spread. Provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Colocasia Cultivars for Florida

common_name: Elena Elephant Ear (Buttery Chartreuse with Purple Veins)

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Elena bears buttery-yellow to chartreuse leaves with purple veining and white-to-purple petioles, coloring brightest in full sun.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun for the brightest color, though it also performs well with some afternoon shade in the hottest part of zone 9. Elena bears luminous buttery-yellow to chartreuse leaves marked with fine purple veining, held on striking white-to-purple petioles that provide additional color contrast against the bright foliage. Its sun-tolerant, glowing color makes it a strong focal point in a bog garden, pond edge, or large container where a bright accent is wanted. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every two to three years to control spread, and keep soil consistently wet.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Colocasia Cultivars for Florida

common_name: Portora Alocasia (Vigorous Glossy Ruffled Bright Green Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Portora is a vigorous, fast-growing Alocasia hybrid that tolerates more sun than most in the genus.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Portora is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. This vigorous hybrid produces large, glossy, ruffled bright green leaves on a fast-growing clump, tolerating more direct sun than most Alocasia without leaf scorch, provided soil stays consistently moist. Its rapid growth and bold, glossy foliage make it a strong statement plant for a tropical-themed border or large container. Protect from cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit, which causes the plant to go dormant or suffer dieback.

common_name: Sarian Alocasia (Dark Green African-Mask Type with Bold White Veins)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sarian bears dark green African-mask-type leaves with dramatic bold white-cream venation.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sarian is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. This African-mask-type Alocasia hybrid bears large, dark green, arrow-shaped leaves boldly marked with thick, bright white-cream venation, an especially dramatic and high-contrast pattern within the popular Alocasia amazonica group of hybrids. Its striking foliage makes a conversation-piece specimen for a shaded patio container or the protected understory of a tropical-themed border. Protect from direct hot sun, which scorches the leaves, and from cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit, which causes the plant to go dormant or suffer dieback.

common_name: Calidora Alocasia (Heat- and Sun-Tolerant Upright Glossy Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Calidora is notably heat- and sun-tolerant for the Alocasia genus.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun. Calidora produces large, upright, glossy medium-green leaves on a robust, fast-growing plant, standing out among Alocasia hybrids for its notable heat and sun tolerance, allowing it to thrive in more exposed Gulf South conditions than most alocasias, which typically need protected shade. Its bold, glossy foliage and vigorous habit make it a strong architectural specimen for a tropical-themed border or large container. Protect from cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit, which causes the plant to go dormant or suffer dieback.

common_name: California Alocasia (Cold-Hardy Heavily Textured Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; California bears large, heavily textured green leaves and is more cold-hardy than many Alocasia selections.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. California bears large, heavily textured, deeply veined green leaves on a robust plant selected for improved cold hardiness and resistance to common Alocasia pests compared to many other selections in the genus, making it a more forgiving choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of Alocasia range. Its bold, textured foliage provides strong architectural presence in a shaded tropical-themed border or large container. Protect from direct hot sun, which scorches the leaves, and mulch heavily over winter in the coolest parts of its range.

common_name: Golden Delicious Elephant Ear (Huge Glowing Chartreuse-Gold Xanthosoma)

planting.note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Delicious bears huge chartreuse-gold arrow-shaped leaves that glow even in shade, tolerating sun to part shade.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Golden Delicious bears huge, arrow-shaped leaves in a glowing chartreuse-gold that lights up a shaded planting even in fairly low light, while also holding up well in brighter exposure, an unusually versatile trait among the large-leaved aroids. As a Xanthosoma rather than Colocasia, it shares the same bold tropical presence and edible-corm background as taro but with this cultivar's foliage grown purely for ornamental impact. The plant spreads by offsets from the main corm; divide every two to three years to control spread, and keep soil consistently moist through the growing season.
